title: Deep Learning Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Deep Learning lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Start with a weighted input
entries.summary: A weight controls how strongly an input affects a calculation. A bias is a number added afterward. A neural network combines many such calculations.

example.code:
input_value = 3
weight = 2
bias = 1
print(input_value * weight + bias)

notes: The word neuron is a loose comparison; this simple calculation is not a whole brain cell.

entries.name: Combine two features
entries.summary: One unit can combine several inputs. Multiply each input by its own weight, add the products, then add the bias.

example.code:
inputs = [2, 3]
weights = [4, 1]
bias = 1
value = sum(x * w for x, w in zip(inputs, weights)) + bias
print(value)

notes: Each feature needs the intended matching weight; order matters.

entries.name: An activation changes the shape
entries.summary: An activation applies a chosen rule after a weighted sum. ReLU keeps positive numbers and changes negative numbers to zero.
notes: ReLU does not turn every output into a probability.

entries.name: Make a small layer
entries.summary: A layer is a group of units that work on the same incoming values. Two units can produce two outputs from one input.

example.code:
x = 3
first = max(0, x * 2 + 1)
second = max(0, x * -1 + 1)
print([first, second])

notes: Two output values do not mean two examples; here one example produced two values.

entries.name: Connect layers in order
entries.summary: A later layer uses the earlier layer outputs as its inputs. Deep networks have several layers that transform information step by step.
notes: Without suitable activations, stacking plain linear layers still gives one overall linear rule.

entries.name: Use shape to check connections
entries.summary: Shape describes how values are arranged. For a batch, each row is one example. A layer must receive the number of features it expects.
notes: Do not mix the number of examples with the number of features.

entries.name: Loss measures a mistake
entries.summary: A loss is a number that measures how wrong a prediction is. Squared error multiplies the difference by itself.
notes: Small training loss alone does not prove good results on new data.

entries.name: A slope points toward a change
entries.summary: A slope describes how quickly a value changes nearby. For the loss (weight - 3) squared, its slope is twice (weight - 3).
notes: A slope is a local guide; a large jump can go past a useful value.

entries.name: Take one learning step
entries.summary: The learning rate sets how big a weight update is. Subtracting a small amount in the slope direction can reduce the loss.

example.code:
weight = 5.0
rate = 0.1
slope = 2 * (weight - 3)
weight = weight - rate * slope
print(round(weight, 2))

notes: A larger learning rate is not always better; it can overshoot.

entries.name: Backpropagation follows the links
entries.summary: Backpropagation finds how each weight affects the loss by following the calculation links backward. Libraries handle this bookkeeping for large networks.

example.code:
Forward: input -> hidden layer -> output -> loss
Backward: loss -> output weights -> hidden weights
Update: use each weight slope to make a small change

notes: Calculating slopes does not itself update weights in every library.

entries.name: Batches and epochs
entries.summary: A batch is a small group of examples processed together. An epoch is one pass through the training set. More passes do not guarantee a better test result.

example.code:
Training set: 12 examples
Batch size: 4 examples
One epoch: 3 batches
Two epochs: 6 batches in total

notes: Do not count an epoch as a new set of data.

entries.name: Check before trusting a network
entries.summary: Training, validation and test sets have different jobs. Validation helps choose settings. The final test checks a choice that has already been made.

example.code:
Training: adjust weights
Validation: choose settings and when to stop
Test: report the final check
Report: describe errors and data limits

notes: A large network can learn unfair or misleading patterns from its data. Check important groups and failure cases.
